Transgenic seeds such as Bt cotton in India and glyphosate-resistant soybeans in Brazil spread rapidly through informal farmer networks outside formal biosafety and intellectual property controls.
Stealth seeds are saved, cross-bred, repackaged, sold, exchanged, and planted in an anarchic agrarian capitalism that defies firm and state surveillance.
The 'terminator technology' narrative in India, linking Monsanto to suicide seeds, was a politically powerful but factually incorrect discourse.
Bt cotton was detected in Gujarat in unauthorized fields under the brand Navbharat 151, which contained the Cry1Ac gene from Monsanto.
The GEAC ordered destruction of unauthorized Bt cotton crops in Gujarat in 2001, but enforcement was weak due to lack of state biosafety committees and political support.
Farmers resisted destruction orders and continued to cultivate and exchange stealth Bt cotton seeds, creating a cottage industry of hybridized variants.
Official Bt cotton seeds are more expensive due to high development and regulatory costs, driving farmers to prefer cheaper stealth seed variants.
By 2005, about 34% of cotton seed packets sold in India were transgenic, with only 9% legal and 25% stealth or illegal varieties.
Stealth seed variants include many branded and unbranded hybrids such as Luxmi, Kavach, Viraat, Sarathi, and generic '151' variants.
Farmers use Navbharat 151 seeds as male parents crossed with local varieties to breed new transgenic hybrids adapted to local conditions.
The Indian Seed Act of 1966, Section 24, protects farmers' rights to save and exchange seeds, including transgenic ones.
Performance of Bt cotton varies widely due to agroecological factors, seed quality, and spurious seeds, but generally shows reduced pesticide use and higher yields.
The GEAC approved three Mahyco-Monsanto Bt cotton varieties in March 2002, making India the 16th country to commercialize genetically engineered plants.
Political support for Bt cotton came from states like Maharashtra, while Gujarat resisted enforcement of biosafety orders.
The underground seed market flourished despite official bans, with some estimates suggesting more than half of transgenic cotton in India comes from unapproved varieties.
Farmers' stealth practices challenge the monopoly power of biotechnology firms and the effectiveness of biosafety and intellectual property regimes.
The failure of regulatory authorities to control stealth seeds reflects the complex political economy of biotechnology governance in India.
The spread of stealth seeds has divided pro-poor political coalitions due to differing views on biotechnology risks and benefits.
The paper suggests that the eventual development of genetic controls like terminator technology is more likely due to the incapacity of social institutions to secure firm and state interests.
Bt cotton farmers in India face a complex decision matrix balancing seed cost, efficacy, and trust in seed sources.
